recipes.title: Lievito Madre Focaccia
recipes.tagline: Overnight counter-rise focaccia for a 46×33 cm sheet pan, made with Molino Rossetto dried lievito madre. Oven 230°C (450°F).

versions.name: Near perfect
versions.summary: About 925 g of dough. Tall and airy but not bready. A bit of a challenge to stretch to the corners.

items.name: All-purpose flour
items.usNote: Spooned and leveled. Grams are more accurate for this dough.

items.name: Molino Rossetto lievito madre powder
items.note: Weigh it. 3 g also works but rises about an hour slower.
items.usNote: No reliable spoon measure for this powder: weigh it.

items.name: Honey
items.note: Crystallized is fine; it dissolves in the water.

items.name: Kosher salt or fine sea salt
items.note: Diamond Crystal, Morton or sea salt: same by weight.
items.usNote: Diamond Crystal. Morton kosher: 2½ tsp. Fine sea salt: 2 tsp. (At batch ×1.)

items.name: Olive oil poured over the dough
Maldon flakes, before baking
items.note: A light sprinkle.

steps.title: Mix (10 pm)
steps.text: Whisk the flour, salt and lievito madre powder in a very large bowl. Stir the honey into the water until dissolved. Add the water and the dough oil to the flour and stir until just combined. Cover.

steps.title: Fold twice (by 11 pm)
steps.text: Rest 30 minutes, then fold with a wet hand: lift one side, stretch it up, lay it over, rotate the bowl, four times. Repeat 30 minutes later. Very sticky at first, much less by the second fold. Don't add flour. Mark the dough level on the bowl.

steps.title: Overnight rise
steps.text: Leave covered at room temperature (about 20°C), wrapped in a blanket, until well risen, about 12 hours. Go by the rise, not the clock.

steps.title: Pan (10 am)
steps.text: Spread the pan oil over the sheet pan. Gently fold the dough onto itself like an envelope and turn it in seam side down. Pour the second oil over it and stretch until it resists. Cover with an upside-down second sheet pan.

steps.title: Rest and stretch (until about 12:30)
steps.text: Every 20–30 minutes, stretch a little further toward the corners, stopping each time it springs back. Continue until it fills the pan and is puffy and jiggly, about 2½ hours.

steps.title: Dimple and brine (about 12:30)
steps.text: Dimple with three fingers at an angle. Dissolve the brine salt in the brine water and pour it over to fill the dimples. Rest 45–60 minutes. Preheat to 230°C (450°F) with a baking stone or inverted sheet pan on the center rack.

steps.title: Bake (about 1:15–1:30)
steps.text: Sprinkle lightly with Maldon. Bake on the stone or inverted pan about 18 minutes, until the bottom is crisp and golden. Then 3–4 minutes on the upper rack to brown the top.

steps.title: Finish and cool
steps.text: Brush with the finishing oil and scatter more Maldon while the surface is oily. Cool 5 minutes in the pan, release with a metal spatula, move to a rack. Slice after 15–20 minutes, top down, with a serrated knife or scissors.

log.text: Dough mixed, with 4 g of powder as insurance on the rise.
Two folds, 30 minutes apart. Very sticky at the first, just right at the second.
Rose on the counter wrapped in a blanket, room 68–69°F. Clearly risen but not doubled at 8–9 hours, so it was left to keep going.
Into the pan, a little over 900 g, covered with a second sheet pan.
Rested and stretched to the corners. A bit of a challenge to stretch fully.
Into the oven. About 18 minutes on the stone, then 3–4 minutes on the top rack.
Mild sprinkle of Maldon before baking, more after baking alongside the finishing oil.

versions.name: Slightly thinner
versions.summary: About 800 g of dough, roughly 13% thinner. Less dough makes the stretch slightly harder, not easier: stretch in stages and rest between them.

items.name: All-purpose flour
items.usNote: Spooned and leveled. Grams are more accurate for this dough.

items.name: Lukewarm water
items.note: 35–40°C. Use 320 g for a less sticky dough.

items.name: Molino Rossetto lievito madre powder
items.note: Weigh it.
items.usNote: No reliable spoon measure for this powder: weigh it.

items.name: Kosher salt or fine sea salt
items.usNote: Diamond Crystal. Morton kosher: 2 tsp. Fine sea salt: 1¾ tsp. (At batch ×1.)

items.name: Olive oil poured over the dough

steps.title: Mix (10 pm)
steps.text: Whisk the flour, salt and lievito madre powder in a very large bowl. Stir the honey into the water until dissolved. Add the water and the dough oil to the flour and stir until just combined. Cover.

steps.title: Fold twice (by 11 pm)
steps.text: Rest 30 minutes, then fold with a wet hand. Repeat 30 minutes later. Mark the dough level on the bowl.

steps.title: Overnight rise
steps.text: Leave covered at about 20°C, wrapped in a blanket, until well risen. Same powder with less flour, so it may be ready up to an hour sooner than the near-perfect version.

steps.title: Pan
steps.text: Spread the pan oil over the sheet pan. Gently fold the dough onto itself and turn it in seam side down. Pour the second oil over it and stretch until it resists. Cover with an upside-down second sheet pan.

steps.title: Rest and stretch
steps.text: Stretch only until it springs back, then leave it 15–20 minutes so the gluten relaxes. Repeat in short sessions until it fills the corners and is puffy and jiggly, about 2–2½ hours. Use plenty of oil underneath.

steps.title: Dimple and brine
steps.text: Dimple, pour the brine over to fill the dimples, and rest 45–60 minutes while the oven and stone heat to 230°C (450°F).

steps.title: Bake
steps.text: Sprinkle lightly with Maldon. Bake on the stone or inverted pan, checking the bottom at 15–16 minutes; it may be done a little before 18. Then 3–4 minutes on the upper rack.

steps.title: Finish and cool
steps.text: Brush with the finishing oil and scatter more Maldon. Cool 5 minutes in the pan, then on a rack. Slice after 15–20 minutes.

notes: Bake time is an estimate until this version has been baked. Record the real time here afterward.

why.head: Dough weight.
why.text: The original recipe made about 1,480 g, roughly 1 g of dough per cm² of pan, which baked into a thick slab. 925 g (about 0.6 g/cm²) is tall and airy; 800 g is thinner still. Below about 750 g it starts to become flatbread.

why.head: The powder is mostly flavor; its yeast does the rising.
why.text: Molino Rossetto lievito madre is 70% dried, inactive sourdough and 30% ordinary dry yeast. 4 g holds about 1.2 g of yeast. That small amount is why the rise takes all night, and the long, slow rise is where most of the flavor comes from.

why.head: Folds instead of kneading.
why.text: Gluten forms on its own once flour is wet, and the long rise does the work kneading would. Folds organize the gluten so it traps gas and holds its shape.

why.head: Why the stretch fights back.
why.text: Stretched gluten pulls back like a rubber band; given time it relaxes and stays put. Stretch in stages, keep plenty of oil underneath, and stretch it warm.

why.head: Maldon on top.
why.text: Thin, hollow flakes sit on the surface and stay crunchy. Small dense kosher crystals dissolve into the brine and add saltiness without crunch.

next: Bake the slightly thinner version and record the real bake time.
Same-day option: about 6 g powder for an 8–9 hour rise, or about 15 g for 4–5 hours somewhere warm. Faster rises taste plainer.
Bread flour, later: more height and chew, but springier and harder to stretch thin. Add about 10 g water. Change one thing at a time.

recipes.title: Buttermilk-Style Pancakes
recipes.tagline: Mark Bittman's basic pancakes, re-leavened for milk soured with lemon when there's no buttermilk. About 12 four-inch pancakes.

versions.name: Lemon-soured milk
versions.summary: From the 7 October 2026 chat. Cup and spoon amounts are the original recipe's; gram weights are converted from them.

items.name: Whole milk
items.note: Start here; add more only if the batter is too stiff to spread.

items.name: Lemon juice
items.note: About half a lemon. White vinegar works the same.

items.name: Baking powder
items.note: Down from 2 tsp in the original.

items.name: Butter or neutral oil, for the pan
items.note: Used across batches.

steps.title: Sour the milk
steps.text: Stir the lemon juice into the milk and leave it alone for 10 minutes. It will thicken slightly and look curdled at the edges. That's the acid denaturing the milk proteins, the same thing that gives real buttermilk its body and tang.

steps.title: Whisk the dry ingredients
steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt and sugar together thoroughly. Whisking matters more than usual here: baking soda is strong and fast, and an unmixed pocket of it tastes soapy and leaves a yellow-brown spot.

steps.title: Whisk the wet ingredients
steps.text: Beat the eggs into the soured milk, then whisk in the melted butter. Make sure the butter has cooled or it will scramble the eggs.

steps.title: Combine, barely
steps.text: Pour the wet into the dry and stir just until no dry flour remains. Lumps are correct. Every extra stroke develops gluten, which is what turns pancakes rubbery. If the batter is too stiff to spread, add milk a tablespoon at a time.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Set a skillet or griddle over medium heat and grease it. It's ready when a drop of water skitters across the surface rather than sitting and sizzling. Cook the batter within about 15 minutes: the soda reacted with the lemon the moment they met, and that lift fades as it sits.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Ladle out scant quarter-cups. Cook until the tops are covered in bubbles and the edges look dry and matte, 2 to 3 minutes.

steps.title: Flip and finish
steps.text: Flip once and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until the second side is golden. Only flip once: pressing down or re-flipping squeezes out the gas you just worked to create.

notes: An earlier chat (July 2026) adapted the same base recipe with 1½ tsp baking powder plus ½ tsp baking soda instead of 1 tsp plus ½ tsp. This card uses the more recent version.

why.head: Why the leavening changed.
why.text: The original's 2 tsp baking powder carries its own acid and needs only moisture and heat. Lemon juice puts free acid in the batter, so half a teaspoon of baking soda does the heavy lifting. Soda is roughly three to four times stronger than powder, but only when there's acid to react with.

why.head: Why keep some baking powder.
why.text: The remaining teaspoon is insurance. Baking powder has a second, heat-triggered stage that fires in the pan, so the pancakes keep rising after the soda's first burst is spent.

why.head: Why start at 1½ cups of milk.
why.text: Soured milk is thinner than true buttermilk, so the lower end of the original range gives a batter with the right body.

recipes.title: Almond, Cardamom & Strawberry Tea Cake
recipes.tagline: Samin Nosrat's almond-paste tea cake from Salt Fat Acid Heat, baked over a caramelized almond topping, with fresh strawberries folded in. One 9-inch (23 cm) round cake. Oven 175°C (350°F).
recipes.credit: Adapted from Salt Fat Acid Heat by Samin Nosrat (Simon & Schuster, 2017). The strawberries are a later addition, not in the original.

versions.name: With strawberries
versions.summary: Not yet made. Gram weights come from the recipe's ounce measures; strawberries and the small spice amounts are converted estimates. Adapted from Salt Fat Acid Heat by Samin Nosrat; the strawberries are a later addition.

items.name: Cake flour
items.note: Set aside about 8 g (1 tbsp) for the strawberries.

items.name: Kosher salt
items.usNote: Diamond Crystal, or ½ tsp fine sea salt.

items.name: Strawberries, sliced
items.note: Optional, but recommended.

steps.title: Prepare the pan
steps.text: Heat the oven to 175°C (350°F) with a rack in the upper third. Butter and flour a 9 by 2-inch (23 by 5 cm) round pan and line the bottom with parchment.

steps.title: Make the almond topping
steps.text: Cook the topping butter and sugar in a small saucepan over medium-high heat for about 3 minutes, until the sugar has dissolved and the butter is bubbling and foamy. Off the heat, stir in the almonds and flaky salt, then spread it evenly over the bottom of the pan. It becomes the top of the cake once it's turned out.

steps.title: Sift the dry ingredients
steps.text: Sift the cake flour, baking powder and salt onto a sheet of parchment, keeping back about a tablespoon of flour for the strawberries. Sifting mixes the leavening evenly and breaks up lumps.

steps.title: Season the eggs
steps.text: Whisk the eggs, vanilla and cardamom together in a small bowl.

steps.title: Grind the almond paste
steps.text: Pulse the almond paste in a food processor to break it up, then add the sugar and run it for about 90 seconds, until it looks like fine sand. A stand mixer works too; give it about 5 minutes.

steps.title: Cream in the butter
steps.text: Add the butter and process until very light and fluffy, at least 2 minutes, scraping down the bowl partway so nothing is left unmixed.

steps.title: Add the eggs slowly
steps.text: With the machine running, add the egg mixture a spoonful at a time, letting the batter turn smooth and glossy again before the next addition. This is an emulsion, like mayonnaise: rush the eggs and the butter can't hold them, and the batter breaks. Scrape the bowl, mix briefly, and move the batter to a large bowl.

steps.title: Fold in flour and fruit
steps.text: Lift the parchment and shake the flour over the batter in three additions, folding gently after each until just combined. Toss the strawberries in the reserved flour, which helps keep them from sinking, and fold them in. Stop as soon as it's mixed; overmixing makes the cake tough.

steps.title: Bake
steps.text: Scrape the batter over the topping and bake about 60 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean and the cake is just pulling away from the sides.

steps.title: Cool and turn out
steps.text: Cool in the pan on a rack. Run a knife around the edge, then warm the bottom of the pan over a burner for a few seconds so the caramelized topping lets go. Turn it out, peel off the parchment, and serve plain or with whipped cream.

notes: Keeps 4 days at room temperature tightly wrapped, or 2 months frozen.
Equipment: food processor (or stand mixer), 9 by 2-inch round cake pan, parchment.

why.head: Almond paste instead of most of the flour.
why.text: The almond paste carries much of the cake's structure and nearly all its moisture, so it needs only a cup of flour. That's why it stays tender for days.

why.head: Eggs a spoonful at a time.
why.text: Butter can only absorb liquid gradually. Added slowly, the eggs stay suspended in the fat as an emulsion; added all at once, the batter curdles and bakes up greasy and dense.

why.head: Cake flour and gentle folding.
why.text: Cake flour is lower in protein, so it forms less gluten. Folding only until combined keeps it that way.

recipes.title: Boma-Style Ghanaian Oxtail Stew
recipes.tagline: Oxtail roasted, then braised low and slow with cumin, coriander, paprika and a tamarind tang, finished with kidney beans and sweet corn. Rebuilt from the ingredient list on Boma's dinner chef's notes card. Serves about 6. Oven 220°C, then 165°C (425°F, then 325°F).
recipes.credit: Reconstructed from the ingredient list on the Boma dinner chef's notes card (Disney's Animal Kingdom Lodge). The card gives ingredients only; every amount and step here is an estimate.

versions.name: Reconstructed
versions.summary: Not yet made. Rebuilt from the ingredient list on Boma's chef's notes card. The card gives no amounts and its order isn't by weight, so every quantity is an estimate. The method follows the card's order. Tamarind and cayenne are the two to adjust to taste.

items.name: Kosher salt
items.usNote: Diamond Crystal. More goes in at the end, to taste.

items.name: Roasted oxtail fat
items.note: From the roasting pan. Top up with neutral oil if the oxtail gave less.

items.name: Cayenne
items.note: Adjust to taste.

items.name: Canned diced tomatoes, with juice
items.note: Doubled from the first draft. Boma describes the dish as tomato-based.

items.name: Water
items.note: Enough to nearly cover the oxtail.

items.name: Beef base (such as Better Than Bouillon)
items.note: A concentrated paste, which is why the card lists water separately.

items.name: Tamarind paste
items.note: Adjust to taste. Add more at the end if the stew tastes flat.

items.name: Red kidney beans, drained and rinsed
items.note: Drained weight of one 439 g (15.5 oz) can.

items.name: Roasted oxtail fat, to finish
items.note: The card lists this second-to-last, just before the cilantro, so it seems to go back in at the end.

steps.title: Season the oxtail
steps.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the oxtail dry and season with the salt and pepper.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Roast in a single layer on a rimmed sheet pan, turning once, until deeply browned, about 45 minutes. Pour off and save the rendered fat; you'll use some now and some at the end. Drop the oven to 165°C (325°F).

steps.title: Sweat the aromatics
steps.text: In a Dutch oven over medium heat, warm 30 g (2 tbsp) of the oxtail fat. Cook the onions and carrots until the onion is soft and golden, about 10 minutes, then add the garlic for 1 minute.

steps.title: Bloom the spices
steps.text: Add the cumin, coriander, paprika and cayenne and stir constantly for about 45 seconds, until fragrant.

steps.title: Fry the tomatoes down
steps.text: Add both cans of tomatoes. Cook, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until they darken from bright red to brick red, thicken, and the fat separates at the edges, about 12 to 15 minutes. This step is borrowed from Ghanaian tomato stews.

steps.title: Build the braising liquid
steps.text: Stir in the water, beef base, tamarind paste and bay leaves, scraping up the browned bits. Add the oxtail and any pan juices; it should be nearly submerged.

steps.title: Braise
steps.text: Bring to a simmer, cover, and move to the oven for about 3 hours, until the meat pulls easily from the bone.

steps.title: Skim
steps.text: Remove the bay leaves and skim the fat off the surface. Better still, chill overnight and lift off the solid fat cap. The stew tastes better the next day anyway.

steps.title: Add beans and corn
steps.text: Bring back to a simmer on the stovetop, add the corn and kidney beans, and simmer about 15 minutes.

steps.title: Thicken and finish
steps.text: Whisk the cornstarch into the cold water, stir it into the simmering stew, and cook 2 minutes until glossy. Stir in about 15 g (1 tbsp) of the reserved roasted fat. Taste and adjust with more salt, and more tamarind if it needs brightness. Top with cilantro and serve over rice.

notes: Reading the card: the chef's ingredient list follows cooking order, not weight. Water comes late here even though it's the heaviest ingredient. So the order can't tell you amounts, but it does give the method: aromatics, then spices, then seasoning, tomato and liquid, then corn, beans and cornstarch late, and the roasted fat and cilantro at the very end.

Only the starred sub-ingredient lines on the card (beef base, diced tomatoes, kidney beans) are by weight. They're copied from packaged-food labels, which US law requires to list ingredients heaviest first.
Despite the name, this is a Disney chef's version. A traditional Ghanaian stew would more likely lean on palm oil, ginger and scotch bonnet.
At Boma it would sit next to the coconut rice or peanut rice on the buffet.

Boma's dish was described in 2021 as a "Western African-inspired tomato-based stew with tamarind" (WDW News Today), which is why this version doubles the tomatoes. An older fan-posted Boma oxtail recipe (2004) is a different dish, with soy sauce, sugar, plantain and a roux.

why.head: Why roast first.
why.text: Dry heat browns the meat (the Maillard reaction), which builds the deep, savory flavor a braise can't make on its own. It also renders fat. The card lists that fat near the end, so some goes back in as a finishing touch: fat carries the roasted flavor that hours of simmering would otherwise mute.

why.head: Why bloom the spices in fat.
why.text: Most of the flavor compounds in cumin, coriander and paprika dissolve in fat, not water. A quick fry releases them; simmering them in liquid alone leaves them dull and dusty.

why.head: Why fry the tomatoes down.
why.text: Cooking off the tomatoes' water concentrates their sugars and browns them, turning a raw, sharp tomato taste into a deep, rounded one. When the fat separates, the water is mostly gone and the base is ready.

why.head: Why three hours.
why.text: Oxtail is mostly connective tissue. Long, gentle heat turns its collagen into gelatin, which makes the meat tender and gives the sauce its silky body.

why.head: Why tamarind.
why.text: Oxtail is very rich. Tamarind's sourness cuts through that richness the way vinegar or citrus would, and it adds a fruity depth.

why.head: Why beans and corn go in late.
why.text: Both are already cooked. Over a three-hour braise they would turn to mush.

recipes.title: Neapolitan Pizza Dough
recipes.tagline: Two-version pizza dough — 60/40 (00/AP) for a lighter, more extensible crust, and 50/50 for a chewier home-oven result. Both use lievito madre plus a small commercial yeast backup, 11 g salt, room-temperature rise. Bake on a preheated steel or stone at 550°F / 290°C.

versions.name: 60/40 — lighter, more extensible
versions.summary: More 00 flour gives a stretchier, thinner dough with better oven spring and more char. Blue bag (Caputo Pizzeria) behaves more extensibly and tears more easily early in the knead — go gently and trust the windowpane test over feel. Developed October 2026.

items.name: Caputo 00 flour
items.note: Red bag (Cuoco) is better for home ovens. Blue bag (Pizzeria) works but tears more during kneading and is optimized for 800°F+ wood-fired.

items.name: All-purpose flour
items.note: King Arthur preferred.

items.name: Fine sea salt
items.note: Mix into flour before adding yeast — never let salt and yeast touch dry.

items.name: Molino lievito madre (dried)
items.note: Dissolve in the water 10–15 min before mixing. Proportional to flour; scale with batch size.

items.name: Extra-virgin olive oil
items.note: About 1 tsp. Plus more for oiling tray and balls.

items.name: Lukewarm water
items.note: ~100°F / 38°C. Dissolve the lievito madre in this first.

steps.title: Dissolve lievito madre
steps.text: Dissolve the lievito madre in the lukewarm water and let sit 10–15 minutes. It should look slightly foamy or cloudy.

steps.title: Mix dry ingredients
steps.text: Whisk both flours together. Add the salt and whisk it in thoroughly.

steps.title: Combine and autolyse
steps.text: Add the lievito madre water and olive oil. Stir until no dry flour remains — the dough will look shaggy and rough. This is correct. Cover tightly and rest 20–25 minutes. The gluten will begin forming on its own; this makes the knead faster and the dough more extensible.

steps.title: Knead
steps.text: Turn onto a very lightly floured surface. Use a slap-fold-rotate motion: slap down, fold toward you, rotate 90°. Use a bench scraper to release the dough from the surface — don't add flour to compensate. With blue bag or after a long autolyse, the dough may tear early; keep going gently, it comes together. After 5–6 minutes, do the windowpane test: pull a small piece slowly — if it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, it's done. The dough will be slightly tacky and may not look as smooth as a red-bag dough. That's fine.

steps.title: Divide and ball
steps.text: Divide into equal pieces. Shape each into a tight ball by folding edges under and pinching at the bottom. Place on a generously oiled tray. Oil the tops lightly and cover tightly with plastic wrap.

steps.title: Rise at room temperature
steps.text: Rise covered until roughly doubled — about 1.5–2.5 hours depending on kitchen temperature. Under a blanket at ~70°F, expect closer to 1.5 hours. Look for visible puffing and a dough that jiggles when you nudge the tray. Don't cut this short — under-risen dough is dense and flat. Optional cold ferment: let the dough puff for 30–45 minutes first, then refrigerate overnight (up to 72 hrs). Bring fully to room temperature before stretching.

steps.title: Stretch and top
steps.text: Rest the balls uncovered 15–20 minutes before stretching. On a floured surface, press and stretch from the center outward — no rolling pin. If it snaps back, cover and wait 10 minutes. Launch from a metal peel dusted generously with semolina (not just flour — semolina acts like ball bearings). Build the pizza quickly and don't let it sit on the peel. Shake the peel to confirm the dough slides freely before launching. Bake on a preheated steel or stone at 550°F / 290°C for 5–7 minutes.

notes: Semolina on the peel is essential with a wet, extensible 00-heavy dough and a metal peel.
For 3 pizzas: scale all ingredients by 1.5. Lievito madre: 22–23g.

versions.name: 50/50 — chewier home-oven result
versions.summary: Equal parts 00 and AP. More forgiving to shape, holds toppings better, chewier crumb. Salt bumped to 11 g from the original 8 g after the 50/50 tasted flat. Developed October 2026.

items.name: Caputo 00 flour
items.note: Red bag (Cuoco) preferred for home ovens.

items.name: All-purpose flour
items.note: King Arthur preferred.

items.name: Fine sea salt
items.note: Mix into flour before adding yeast.

items.name: Molino lievito madre (dried)
items.note: Dissolve in the water 10–15 min before mixing.

items.name: Extra-virgin olive oil
items.note: About 1 tsp. Plus more for oiling.

steps.title: Dissolve lievito madre
steps.text: Dissolve the lievito madre in the lukewarm water and let sit 10–15 minutes.

steps.title: Mix dry ingredients
steps.text: Whisk both flours together with the salt.

steps.title: Combine and autolyse
steps.text: Add the lievito madre water and olive oil. Stir until no dry flour remains. Cover and rest 20–25 minutes.

steps.title: Knead
steps.text: Knead 6–8 minutes using the slap-fold-rotate method. Use a bench scraper to manage sticking. The 50/50 dough gets noticeably smoother than a 60/40. Finish with the windowpane test.

steps.title: Divide, ball, and rise
steps.text: Same as the 60/40 version: divide, ball tightly, oil tray and tops, cover, rise at room temperature until doubled (1.5–2.5 hours). Same cold ferment option applies.

steps.title: Stretch and top
steps.text: Rest 15–20 minutes before stretching. The 50/50 is stiffer and less likely to tear. Semolina on the peel still recommended. Bake at 550°F / 290°C for 5–7 minutes.

notes: The original recipe used 8 g salt and commercial yeast only at ½ tsp. The salt was bumped to 11 g and the yeast switched to lievito madre exclusively after the madre proved reliable.
The 50/50 handles heavier toppings better than the 60/40 and is easier to stretch for beginners.

why.head: Why two flours.
why.text: 00 flour is finely milled and produces a silky, extensible dough that stretches without snapping. AP flour is coarser and adds chew and structure. The 60/40 leans toward extensibility and oven spring; the 50/50 leans toward a chewier, more forgiving dough.

why.head: Why lievito madre.
why.text: Lievito madre (dried sourdough starter) provides flavor — slow fermentation builds complexity that commercial yeast alone can't match. At room temperature under a blanket it gives a reliable 1.5–2.5 hour rise once it's proven active.

why.head: Why 11 g salt.
why.text: The original recipe used 8 g (about 2.6% of flour weight). After baking, the crust tasted flat. 11 g brings it to about 3.6%, near the top of the traditional Neapolitan range, and the difference is noticeable.

why.head: Why autolyse before kneading.
why.text: Gluten forms when flour and water combine, even without kneading. Letting the dough rest 20–25 minutes after mixing means the gluten is already partially developed before kneading starts — less work, better texture, more extensible result.

why.head: Why semolina on the peel.
why.text: A wet 00-heavy dough on a metal peel sticks badly. Semolina is coarser than flour and acts like ball bearings under the dough. Always shake the peel before launching to confirm the dough slides freely.

next: Bake the 60/40 version with red bag (Cuoco) and compare to blue bag.
Try cold ferment with the lievito madre formula and record the difference in flavor.
Test 70/30 ratio for even more extensibility at higher oven temperatures.
